load.name: Load images
load.desc: Pick the folder where your telescope or camera saved the images. Light, dark and flat frames are sorted automatically. You can also pick a single, already stacked image.

stack.name: Stack images
stack.desc: Many short exposures are combined into one much cleaner image. The frames are aligned precisely on the stars; dark and flat frames remove the sensor's own flaws.

align.label: Align images on the stars
align.help: Turn off if the images already line up exactly (e.g. an already stacked image).

reject.label: Skip poor frames automatically
reject.help: Frames that moved, were clouded out or show too few stars are left out.

gradient.label: Remove background gradient per frame
gradient.help: Under light-polluted skies the gradient shifts during the night; removing it per frame gives a cleaner average.

framing.label: Keep the full field of view
framing.help: Rotated frames can leave darker corners – crop them in the next step. When off, the result is cut to the reference frame.

clip.label: Filter outliers (satellite trails, hot pixels)
clip.help: Averages in two passes: the second pass drops values far from the mean. Slower but cleaner.

crop.name: Crop
crop.desc: Drag a rectangle over the part of the image you want to keep. If you select nothing, the thin faulty band left by stacking at the edges is removed.

margin.label: Trim edges
margin.help: The slider sets the selection shown on the image; you can fine-tune its edges with the mouse afterwards.

rotate.label: Rotate
rotate.help: Quarter turns – lossless. The preview follows immediately; you draw the selection on the rotated image.

angle.label: Fine rotation
angle.help: Straighten the image by any angle; the corners stay empty and the selection cuts them away.

bge.name: Flatten background
bge.desc: Light pollution and the Moon leave an uneven, blotchy background. Here it is smoothed out so the sky is equally dark everywhere.

method.label: Method
method.help: The AI model recognises nebulae and galaxies and removes only the true background. The polynomial is simpler but needs a careful setting when a large object fills the frame.

model.label: AI model
model.help: Leave empty to use the newest model available.

smoothing.label: Smoothing
smoothing.help: Fine: the model follows smaller blotches too. Coarse: only the large, slow gradient is removed.

strength.label: Flattening strength (polynomial)
strength.help: Polynomial method only: how bright an area may be and still count as background.

correction.label: Correction
correction.help: Subtraction fixes light-pollution gradients; division fixes vignetting (darker corners).

deconv.name: Sharpen
deconv.desc: The atmosphere and the optics blur the details slightly. Sharpening reverses that as far as possible. Stars are tightened first, then the detail of nebulae and galaxies is brought out – each with its own AI model.

stars.label: Sharpen stars
stars.help: Stars become smaller and more point-like.

object.label: Sharpen nebula, galaxy
object.help: Fine structure (dust lanes, spiral arms) becomes more defined.

objectStrength.label: Nebula, galaxy – strength
objectStrength.help: Too much also amplifies noise – if it turns grainy, back off.

starsModel.label: AI model (stars)
starsModel.help: Leave empty to use the newest model available.

objectModel.label: AI model (nebula, galaxy)
objectModel.help: Leave empty to use the newest model available.

autoPsf.label: Measure star size automatically
autoPsf.help: The model needs to know how large the stars are (FWHM). When off, set it with the slider.

denoise.name: Reduce noise
denoise.desc: Long exposures and high ISO make the image grainy. The AI model smooths the grain while stars and fine detail are kept.

strength.label: Strength
strength.help: How much of the denoised version is mixed into the original. Full: only the model output; lower values leave a more natural grain.

model.label: AI model
model.help: Leave empty to use the newest model available.

platesolve.name: Identify the sky
platesolve.desc: From the star pattern we work out exactly where the image points: Gaia catalogue stars around the direction the telescope wrote into the header are matched to the image (from an offline catalogue or the internet). Needed for accurate colour calibration.

object.label: Object name
object.help: Pre-filled from the image header (or the folder name). If the header has a direction it is used; otherwise – or if you type a different name – this name is looked up online (e.g. M 31, NGC 6992, IC 1396).

scale.label: Pixel scale (″/px, if the header has none)
scale.help: Leave empty to compute it from the focal length and pixel size. Seestar S50: 2.3.

maglimit.label: Catalogue magnitude limit
maglimit.help: Dense star fields need only the brighter stars; sparse fields need a fainter limit.

platesolve.online: No offline catalogue – fetched from the internet (the server is sometimes slow).

colorcal.name: Calibrate colours
colorcal.desc: The stars on the image are compared with their colours measured by the Gaia catalogue, and the red and blue channels are scaled so that a Sun-like star comes out white. Nebulae and galaxies then show their true colours. Needs the sky identification step.

white.label: What should be white?
white.help: The usual choice is Sun-like white – galaxies look natural with a slightly warm tone. Vega-white gives a cooler, bluer image.

neutral.label: Neutralise background
neutral.help: Also balances the colour of the sky background so it has no tint anywhere.

starremoval.name: Separate stars
starremoval.desc: The stars are moved to a separate layer temporarily, so nebula and stars can each be brought out in the way that suits them. This uses the free StarNet2 program, which you download once.
starremoval.missing: StarNet2 is not installed or could not be found. Click the setup button – it explains what it is and where to download it.

ghs.name: Bring out nebulae and galaxies
ghs.desc: The raw image is almost black: the faint detail hides in the dark. Here it is brought out – with the same sliders as Siril's GHS stretch. The image and the histogram follow the settings live; "Apply" commits the stretch and starts the next one from a clean slate, so you can work in several gentle passes.

lnD.label: Stretch factor (ln(D+1))
lnD.help: How much contrast is added around the symmetry point – the main slider. Zero = no change.

b.label: Local stretch intensity (b)
b.help: How concentrated the contrast is around the symmetry point: large b = narrow, strong boost; small or negative b = wider, softer.

sp.label: Symmetry point (SP)
sp.help: The brightness where the contrast boost is largest. Small (near the background) for faint nebulosity, larger for a bright core.

lp.label: Shadow protection point (LP)
lp.help: Below this the stretch stays linear – background noise is not amplified. At most SP.

hp.label: Highlight protection point (HP)
hp.help: Above this the stretch stays linear – bright parts do not burn out. At least SP.

bp.label: Black point (BP)
bp.help: Linear type only: this much is subtracted, the background gets darker.

colour.label: Colour model
colour.help: The luminance models keep the colour ratios (stars and nebulae do not wash out); independent channels is Siril's classic behaviour.

ghs.none: No stretch committed yet – set the sliders and press Apply.

starstretch.name: Stretch stars
starstretch.desc: The stars are brightened separately and more gently so they stay small and colourful instead of white blobs.

recombine.name: Put stars back
recombine.desc: The separately enhanced nebula and the separately stretched stars are combined again. The slider sets the weight of the stars: fewer stars make the nebula stand out more.

green.name: Remove green cast
green.desc: There are no green nebulae in space – if your image looks greenish, that is the sensor. It is removed here; other colours stay untouched.

fringe.name: Fix colour fringes
fringe.desc: Bright stars may show a purple or blue fringe caused by the optics. Here it is faded out.

contrast.name: Contrast
contrast.desc: Slightly deeper darks, slightly livelier lights – the image "comes together". Careful: too much contrast swallows faint nebulosity.

saturation.name: Saturation
saturation.desc: The reds and blues of the nebulae and the colours of the stars become a little more vivid. Brightness is unchanged.

save.name: Save
save.desc: Your image is ready! Choose what you want to use it for; we set the rest.

welcome.title: Welcome to ClearStar!
welcome.lead: From raw frames to a finished astrophoto in three moves. We hold your hand all the way and explain what happens at every step.
welcome.s1sub: One folder is enough; we handle the rest.
welcome.s3sub: For sharing, printing or further editing.

catalog.title: Offline star catalogue
catalog.whatTitle: What is it and why is it useful?
catalog.what: Sky identification and colour calibration need a star catalogue (Gaia DR3). By default it is fetched from the internet, but the Gaia servers are sometimes slow or do not answer – then the step gets stuck. With a once-downloaded offline catalogue (about 1.5 GB) both steps run without internet in about a second. It is the same file Siril uses: if you already downloaded it there, it is found automatically.
catalog.howTitle: How to get it (once, about 5–10 minutes)
catalog.how:
Click "Download now": ClearStar downloads it (1.1 GB compressed), unpacks it (1.5 GB), verifies the file and starts using it automatically. You can keep working meanwhile.

If you already have the file (e.g. downloaded for Siril), point to it with "Choose catalogue file…". The catalogue is the Siril team's Gaia DR3 extract (Siril Astrometry Catalogue, CC BY 4.0, Zenodo; Gaia data: ESA/Gaia/DPAC, CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO).
catalog.downloaded: Done: the catalogue is downloaded and verified.
catalog.missing: No offline catalogue – sky identification works over the internet (when the server answers).
catalog.invalid: This file is not a Siril HEALPix astrometric catalogue (siril_cat_healpix8_astro.dat).
catalog.sirilNote: If you have already set it up in Siril, it is picked up automatically.

starnet.title: Set up StarNet2
starnet.whatTitle: What is it and why is it needed?
starnet.what: StarNet2 is a free, AI-based program that separates the stars from the image. Astrophotographers do this because faint nebulae and galaxies can be brought out much more strongly when the stars do not bloat along the way – at the end the stars are put back separately and gently. ClearStar runs this program in the background; you only need to download it once.
starnet.how:
1. Open the download page with the button below and get the Windows command-line version (StarNet2 CLI, Windows – "ONNX" or "x64 cli" in the file name; it runs on the graphics card too).
2. Unpack it into a permanent folder, e.g. D:\astro\starnet (or run the installer).
3. Click "Choose StarNet2…" and point to starnet2.exe in that folder.

The program is free to use for astrophoto processing; ClearStar does not include or distribute it.
starnet.missing: Not set up yet – ClearStar also checked Siril's settings and the usual install locations.
starnet.sirilNote: If you have already set it up in Siril, it is picked up automatically.

about.title: About
about.tagline: Beginner-friendly astrophoto processing – from raw frames to the finished photo, step by step.
about.languageNote: The language change takes effect when the program restarts. New language: copy an xx.json file to:
about.gpu: Run AI models on the graphics card (DirectML)
about.gpuNote: When on, sharpening and background extraction are many times faster on any DirectX 12 graphics card (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel). If it causes trouble, turn it off – the CPU works too, just slower.
about.summary: ClearStar is the author's own work; the code is free to use, modify and redistribute under the GNU GPL 3.0 (or later). The stacking, stretching and background-extraction methods were written after studying the source code of Siril and GraXpert (both GPL-3.0) – no code was copied. The AI steps use the GraXpert Development Team's models, licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0: they may be used for non-commercial purposes only and are not included in ClearStar. The images you create with the program are yours. The program sends no data anywhere; the network is used only for model downloads you request. Details and the list of contributors are on the other tabs.
